walkthroughs.title: Market, limit, stop
steps: A market order says: fill me now at the best price available. The fill is close to sure. The price isn't.
A limit order says: my price or better. You control the price, but it may never fill.
A stop order waits. When price reaches the stop price, it becomes a market order.
A stop-limit becomes a limit order instead. Your price is protected, but the fill isn't.

walkthroughs.title: How long it lives, how much fills
steps: Every order has a time in force. Pick nothing and it's usually a day order.
A day order that doesn't fill generally cancels at the close. It won't carry into after-hours or tomorrow.
Good 'til canceled stays live until it fills or you cancel, within your broker's time limit.
IOC takes what fills now and cancels the rest. FOK is all of it now, or nothing.

walkthroughs.title: Short words
steps: A short sale sells shares you don't own. Your broker usually lends them to you, and the loan can carry a fee.
Before the short, the broker needs a locate: good reason to believe the shares can be borrowed.
To close a short you buy the shares back. That's covering, entered as buy to cover.
When many shorts cover at once, their buying pushes price higher. That's a short squeeze.

questions.q: What does a market order tell your broker?
choices: Trade now at the best price available
Trade only at my limit price or better
Trade once the price hits my trigger
Trade at the day's closing price
questions.answer: Trade now at the best price available
questions.why: Trade now at the best price available. The SEC says a market order generally executes right away. The price it fills at is not guaranteed. FINRA says it gives the most certainty of a fill. The trade-off: a likely fill, not a set price.
questions.lesson_line: A market order is about the fill, not the price.

wrong.Trade only at my limit price or better: That's a limit order. It protects your price and may never fill.
wrong.Trade once the price hits my trigger: That's a stop order. It waits for the stop price, then becomes a market order.
wrong.Trade at the day's closing price: That's an on-close order, a separate instruction you have to choose.

questions.simple: A market order says trade now at the best price you can get, so it usually fills fast, at no promised price.

reasons: fixed before (2026-11-10 variety rewrite)

questions.q: Unless you choose otherwise, brokers typically enter an order as a market order.
questions.why: True. FINRA says brokers typically enter a market order unless you specify otherwise, and the SEC glossary says the same. 'Typically' matters: platforms can differ, so check what your own ticket is set to. A market order sets no price, and its fill price is not guaranteed.
questions.lesson_line: Read the order type before you send. A market order sets no price limit.
questions.simple: True, if you do not pick an order type, brokers usually send a market order, so check your ticket first.

reasons: a broker convention ('typically'), not a rule; individual platform presets were not surveyed

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A buyer will pay $25.40 and not a cent more, so they use a ___ order.
questions.why: Limit. A limit order trades only at your price or better. For a buy, that means the limit price or lower, so $25.40 is the most the buyer pays. The trade-off: a limit order is not guaranteed to fill at all.
questions.lesson_line: A limit order names your price. The trade-off is that it may never fill.
questions.simple: Limit, because a buy limit can only fill at its price or lower, so the buyer never pays more than $25.40.

questions.q: A sell limit order at $30.00 can fill at $29.90.
questions.why: False. A sell limit can only fill at the limit price or higher. $29.90 is below the $30.00 limit, so it cannot fill there. It can fill above $30.00, never below it.
questions.lesson_line: Buy limit: your price or lower. Sell limit: your price or higher.
questions.simple: False, a sell limit at $30.00 only sells at $30.00 or higher, and $29.90 is lower.

questions.q: On a limit order, what is the limit price?
choices: The worst price you'll accept
The price that triggers the order
The price you're sure to get
The last trade before you sent it
questions.why: The worst price you'll accept. A limit order buys or sells at a set price or better. If it fills, you get the limit price or better, never worse. For a buy, better means lower. For a sell, better means higher. The limit does not promise a fill. The order may never execute.
questions.lesson_line: The limit is your line in the sand. Better can happen. Worse can't.

wrong.The price that triggers the order: That's the stop price on a stop or stop-limit order.
wrong.The price you're sure to get: Nothing is sure. A limit order may not fill at all, and it can fill better.
wrong.The last trade before you sent it: That's the last sale price. Your limit is a price you set, not one the market hands you.

questions.simple: The limit price is the worst price you will take, because a limit order fills only at that price or better.

questions.q: What kind of limit order is that?
questions.story: The quote is $10.00 bid, $10.05 ask. You send a buy limit order at $10.10.
choices: Marketable: it can fill right away
Non-marketable: it waits for a seller
A stop-limit waiting on a trigger
Non-marketable: it fills only at $10.10
questions.answer: Marketable: it can fill right away
questions.why: Marketable. Under the SEC's rule text, a buy limit priced at or above the best offer is a marketable limit order. Your $10.10 limit is above the $10.05 ask, so it can trade right away. It still caps your price. A buy limit fills only at the limit or lower, so you never pay more than $10.10. Marketable is judged when the order arrives, against the best offer then.
questions.lesson_line: A buy limit at or above the ask is marketable. It acts fast and still caps your price.

wrong.Non-marketable: it waits for a seller: That would be a buy limit below the ask, at the bid for example. Yours already reaches the sellers.
wrong.A stop-limit waiting on a trigger: There's no stop price here. It's a plain limit order, live as soon as you send it.
wrong.Non-marketable: it fills only at $10.10: A buy limit fills at the limit or lower, not only at it. Priced above the $10.05 ask, it can trade at once.

questions.simple: It is marketable, because a buy limit at or above the ask can fill right away and still caps your price.

questions.q: What does a stop order do?
choices: Becomes a market order at a trigger
Fills only at your price or better
Cancels unless it is filled right away
Sells at exactly the stop price shown
questions.answer: Becomes a market order at a trigger
questions.why: Becomes a market order at a trigger. A stop order, also called a stop-loss order, waits until price reaches the stop price. Then it becomes a market order. The stop price is the trigger, not a promised fill price, so the fill can come in worse. A sell stop sits below the current price, a buy stop above it.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger. Once it fires, you get the market.

wrong.Sells at exactly the stop price shown: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill. The fill can come in worse.

questions.simple: A stop order waits for its trigger price, then turns into a market order, so the fill price is not promised.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Another name for a stop order is a ___ order.
questions.why: Stop-loss. The SEC says a stop order is 'also referred to as a stop-loss order'. Same order, two names. A stop-limit is a different order: at the stop price it becomes a limit order, not a market order.
questions.lesson_line: Stop and stop-loss name the same order.
questions.simple: Stop-loss, because the SEC says a stop order is also called a stop-loss order.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (SEC f7, Tier 1)

questions.q: On a stop order, what is the stop price?
choices: The price that sets the order off
The price your shares will sell at
The worst price you'll accept
Your average cost on the trade
questions.answer: The price that sets the order off
questions.why: The price that sets the order off. FINRA calls the stop price the 'trigger' price. When it is reached, a stop order becomes a market order. The SEC says the stop price is not the guaranteed execution price.
questions.lesson_line: Stop price means trigger. It is not the price you get.

wrong.The price your shares will sell at: Not promised. The stop turns into a market order, and the fill can be worse.
wrong.The worst price you'll accept: That's a limit price. A plain stop has no limit.
wrong.Your average cost on the trade: That's your cost. A stop price sits wherever you choose to put it.

questions.simple: It is the trigger price, the level that sets the order off, not the price you are sure to get.

questions.q: A stop-loss order caps your loss at the stop price.
questions.why: False. A stop-loss is a stop order. At the stop price it becomes a market order, and the stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill. In a fast market, or when price gaps past the stop, the fill can be far worse.
questions.lesson_line: The name sounds like a promise. It's a trigger, and gaps and fast markets go right through it.
questions.simple: False, at the stop price the order becomes a market order, so a fast move or a gap can fill it worse.

deeper.trap: The name 'stop-loss' sounds like a cap on the loss. It is not. FINRA warns that in volatile markets a stop may be executed at a price significantly different from the stop price. Schwab notes a short's stop could lock in significant losses if the price gaps up. The stop decides when you get out, not the price you get.

reasons: fixed before (why sentence split)

questions.q: Which order sits above the current price and becomes a market order once price rises to it?
choices: Buy stop
Buy limit
Sell stop
Sell limit
questions.why: Buy stop. A buy stop is entered at a stop price above the current market price. When price rises to it, it becomes a market order to buy. It can limit a loss on a short, or open a position once price reaches a level. A buy limit is different. It pays your price or lower, so one placed above the price can fill at once.
questions.lesson_line: A buy stop waits above the price. A rise to it fires a market buy.

wrong.Buy limit: A buy limit fills at your price or lower. Placed above the price, it can fill right away instead of waiting.
wrong.Sell stop: A sell stop sits below the price, to sell shares you own.
wrong.Sell limit: A sell limit stays a limit order. It sells at your price or higher and does not turn into a market order.

questions.simple: A buy stop sits above the price and becomes a market buy when the price rises to it.

questions.q: Which order does that?
questions.story: You sold a stock short at $30. You want out automatically if it rises to $32.
choices: A buy stop at $32
Sell stop at $32
Buy limit at $32
A sell limit $32
questions.why: A buy stop at $32. You're short, so getting out means buying. A buy stop sits above the current price. If the stock rises to it, it becomes a market buy and closes the short. The stop price is a trigger, not a promised price. In a fast move or a gap up, the fill can come in above $32.
questions.lesson_line: Short a stock and your stop is a buy stop above. Set it when you enter.

wrong.Sell stop at $32: A sell stop sells, and it sits below the price. You're short, so getting out means buying.
wrong.Buy limit at $32: A buy limit fills at $32 or lower. The stock is below $32 now, so it could buy at once instead of waiting for a rise.
wrong.A sell limit $32: You own no shares, so selling at $32 is another short sale. It adds to the short instead of closing it.

questions.simple: Use a buy stop at $32, because you close a short by buying and a buy stop fires on a rise.

questions.q: What happened to your shares?
questions.story: Your sell stop sits at $45. At 10 a.m. the stock trades down to $44.80 for a few minutes, then rallies. It closes at $47.
choices: The stop sold them on the dip
Nothing, stops wait for the close
They sold later, at the $47 close
Nothing, the dip was too brief
questions.answer: The stop sold them on the dip
questions.why: The stop sold them on the dip. A sell stop triggers once price reaches the stop price during the day, then becomes a market order. A short intraday move is enough. The rally and the $47 close don't undo the sale.
questions.lesson_line: A stop doesn't wait for the close. A brief dip through it is enough to set it off.

wrong.Nothing, stops wait for the close: A stop triggers when price reaches it during the day. It doesn't wait for the close.
wrong.They sold later, at the $47 close: Once the dip set it off, the stop became a market order and sold then, not at the close.
wrong.Nothing, the dip was too brief: FINRA says rapid price movement during a short period of time could trigger a stop. A few minutes at $44.80 is enough.

questions.simple: The stop sold them, because a stop fires as soon as price reaches it, even for a few minutes.

deeper.trap: A $47 close makes the $45 stop look safe. It was not. The SEC warns a short-term, intraday move can trigger a stop. The fill can be substantially worse than the day's close. So choose the stop price with care.

questions.q: What is a stop-limit order?
choices: A stop that becomes a limit order
A limit order with no time limit
A stop that follows the price up
A stop that fills all or none of it
questions.answer: A stop that becomes a limit order
questions.why: A stop that becomes a limit order. Once the stop price is reached, a stop-limit becomes a limit order. It then fills only at your limit price or better. The stop price and the limit price don't have to be the same. The catch is the fill. If price moves past your limit, the order may not execute.
questions.lesson_line: Stop-limit: the stop says when, the limit says how bad a price you'll take.

wrong.A limit order with no time limit: That's a limit order marked good 'til canceled (GTC).
wrong.A stop that fills all or none of it: All-or-none is a size condition, not a stop-limit.

questions.simple: A stop-limit waits for its stop price, then becomes a limit order that fills only at your limit or better.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: Which order says exactly that?
questions.story: A trader owns 300 shares, trading at $42. They want out if it falls to $40, but won't sell below $39.50, even if that means no sale.
choices: Sell stop-limit: stop $40, limit $39.50
Sell a plain stop order at $40, no limit
Sell limit at $39.50, as a day order
Sell trailing stop with a $0.50 trail
questions.why: A sell stop-limit with a $40 stop and a $39.50 limit. At $40 it becomes a limit order, so it can only sell at $39.50 or better. The SEC says the stop and limit prices need not match. The cost: it may not sell at all.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-limit has two prices: the stop sets it off, and the limit guards the price.

wrong.Sell limit at $39.50, as a day order: That's below the price, so it can sell right away. It doesn't wait for $40.
wrong.Sell trailing stop with a $0.50 trail: That stop follows price up and sits only $0.50 under it. It isn't the $40 trigger the trader wants.
wrong.Sell a plain stop order at $40, no limit: A plain stop becomes a market order at $40 and can sell below $39.50 in a fast drop.

questions.simple: A stop-limit, because at $40 it turns into a limit order that will not sell below $39.50.

deeper.trap: A stop-limit can leave you holding a falling stock. FINRA says it trades only if the limit price or better can be had after the stop is hit. Schwab warns that with a stop-limit a trader risks missing the market altogether. If the stock drops through $39.50 fast, this order sits unfilled while the loss grows.

reasons: fixed before (Sell prefix restored on the key)

questions.q: In a fast drop straight through both prices, a sell stop-limit can leave you still holding the stock.
questions.why: True. Once the stop price is hit, a stop-limit becomes a limit order. If price falls through your limit before it fills, the order can sit unfilled and you still own the stock. It can also fill in part. That is the trade-off. A stop-limit protects your price. A plain stop gets you out whatever the price.
questions.lesson_line: If getting out matters most, a stop-limit can fail you. Know which you need before the drop.
questions.simple: True, because once triggered it is a limit order, and if price falls past your limit it may never fill.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a stop-limit is a safer stop. It protects the price, not the exit. In a fast drop or a gap through both prices, the limit is left behind. You can still hold the stock after it falls. Schwab warns that with a stop-limit a trader risks missing the market altogether. FINRA says to choose a stop-limit when the price matters more than getting out.

questions.q: What is a trailing stop?
choices: A stop that follows price by a gap
A stop parked at your entry price
A stop that only counts at the close
A stop that turns into a limit order
questions.answer: A stop that follows price by a gap
questions.why: A stop that follows price by a set gap. The SEC says the gap is a set percent or dollar amount from the market price. When price moves your way, the stop follows. When price turns against you, it stays put and triggers if price reaches it.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop moves one way only: in your favor.

wrong.A stop parked at your entry price: A stop at your entry is a fixed level. A trailing stop follows price only when it moves your way.
wrong.A stop that only counts at the close: Stops trigger when price reaches them during the day.
wrong.A stop that turns into a limit order: That's a stop-limit. A plain trailing stop becomes a market order. What makes it trailing is that its stop price follows the market.

questions.simple: A trailing stop follows the price by a set gap as price moves your way, and stays put when it turns.

reasons: fixed before (stop-limit note reworded)

questions.q: You buy at $30 and set a sell trailing stop $2 below the price. It climbs to $37.40, then dips to $36. Where is your stop now?
questions.why: $35.40. A trailing stop follows the high by the set amount: $37.40 less $2. When price dips to $36, the stop does not move down. It holds at $35.40, and the $36 dip is still above it, so nothing triggers.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop tracks the high, not your entry.
questions.simple: Your stop is at $35.40, because it trails the $37.40 high by $2 and does not drop on the dip.

reasons: computed key (calc)

wrong.$28.00: Trailed from your $30 entry, not from the high.
wrong.$37.40: Gave the high and forgot to take off the $2.
wrong.$34.00: Trailed from the $36 dip, not from the high.

questions.q: When the stock drops, a sell trailing stop can move down with it.
questions.why: False. A sell trailing stop moves only when price moves your way, which is up. When price drops, the trailing stop price stays fixed. The order triggers if price falls to it. On a long position, it never adjusts lower.
questions.lesson_line: Up, it follows. Down, it waits for you at the line.
questions.simple: False, because a sell trailing stop only moves up with the price and stays put when the stock falls.

questions.q: What's the likely problem?
questions.story: You set a sell trailing stop $0.25 below the price. The stock normally swings about $2 in a day. Your plan is to hold for weeks.
choices: Small dips will trigger it
It waits for the day's close
It turns into a limit order
It moves down on red days
questions.why: Small dips will trigger it. The SEC warns that short-term moves in a stock's price can set off a trailing stop. A $0.25 trail on a stock that swings about $2 a day sits inside its normal daily range. A small dip after any new high can trigger it, long before a weeks-long plan plays out. Once triggered, a plain trailing stop becomes a market order.
questions.lesson_line: A trail tighter than the stock's normal swing gets hit by ordinary noise.

wrong.It turns into a limit order: A plain trailing stop becomes a market order when it triggers.
wrong.It moves down on red days: It never moves down. On a drop it holds still.
wrong.It waits for the day's close: It triggers when price reaches it, and an intraday move can do that. With a trail that tight, that's almost any dip.

questions.simple: A $0.25 trail is far tighter than the stock's normal $2 daily swing, so small, ordinary dips will trigger it.

deeper.trap: A tight trail feels safer because it gives back less. But the SEC says short-term fluctuations can activate a trailing stop. If the stock swings about $2 a day, a $0.25 trail gets hit by ordinary noise. Once triggered, a plain trailing stop becomes a market order. The SEC's advice is to select the trailing stop price carefully.

questions.q: Where does your buy stop trigger?
questions.story: You're short at $40 with a $3 trailing buy stop. The stock falls to a low of $31, then bounces.
choices: At $34
At $43
At $37
At $31
questions.why: At $34. A trailing buy stop follows the stock's lowest price down, staying $3 above it. Each new low pulls it lower, and it does not move back up. From the $31 low, it sits at $34 and triggers if the stock rises there.
questions.lesson_line: On a short the trail follows the lows. Every new low pulls your stop down.

wrong.At $43: That's $3 above your entry, where it started. It moved down as the stock fell.
wrong.At $37: That's your entry minus the trail. On a short the stop sits above the price, and it trails the low.
wrong.At $31: That's the low itself. The stop sits the $3 trail above the low, and triggers only on a rise of $3 or more off it.

questions.simple: At $34, because on a short the trailing stop sits $3 above the lowest price, and the low was $31.

deeper.trap: On a short, everything flips. A long's trailing stop rides under the highs. A short's trailing buy stop rides above the lows. As the stock falls from $40 to $31, the stop falls with it, from $43 to $34. It never climbs back on the bounce, so a bounce of $3 or more off the low triggers it.

reasons: computed key (calc)
trailing buy stop mechanics come from one Tier 2 publisher (Schwab f86, f87); the SEC f17 covers the general trail

questions.q: What is a bracket order?
choices: An entry with linked stop and target
Two orders where one cancels the other
A stop that follows the price up
An order to buy within a price range
questions.answer: An entry with linked stop and target
questions.why: An entry with a linked stop and target. A bracket wraps an entry with two opposite-side orders. Once the entry fills, a take-profit limit and a protective stop go in. They are linked as an OCO, so one filling cancels the other. On a buy, the sell limit sits above and the sell stop below. Fidelity calls the same structure one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other.
questions.lesson_line: A bracket puts the whole plan on the ticket: entry, stop, target.

wrong.Two orders where one cancels the other: That's an OCO. A bracket uses an OCO for its exits, but it starts with the entry.
wrong.An order to buy within a price range: The name sounds like a range, but it isn't one. A bracket is one entry plus a linked stop and target.

questions.simple: A bracket is an entry with a stop and a profit target attached, linked so one filling cancels the other.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: What kind of order did you send?
questions.story: A stock trades at $25.40. You send one ticket: buy 200 shares at market. When it fills, a sell limit at $28.00 and a sell stop at $24.20 go in, linked.
choices: Bracket order
Trailing stop
Stop-limit order
Fill-or-kill
questions.why: Bracket order. One ticket opens the trade. When the entry fills, a take-profit limit above and a stop below go in, linked as an OCO. When one exit fills, the other cancels. Fidelity calls the same structure one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other.
questions.lesson_line: With a bracket, the stop is in the moment you're filled.

wrong.Trailing stop: A trailing stop is one exit that moves with price. This ticket has an entry and two fixed exits.
wrong.Stop-limit order: A stop-limit is one order with two prices. This is three linked orders.
wrong.Fill-or-kill: Fill-or-kill is a size and timing condition: all of it now, or cancel.

questions.simple: It is a bracket order, because one ticket buys and then puts in a linked profit target and stop.

questions.q: What does an OCO order do?
choices: Two orders: one fills, other cancels
One order: all of the shares or none
One order fills, then triggers a second
Cancels if not filled right away
questions.answer: Two orders: one fills, other cancels
questions.why: Two orders: one fills, the other cancels. An OCO pairs two live orders. When either one executes, the other is canceled automatically. One use is a profit target and a protective stop on the same shares, so both exits can't fire. It is not one-triggers-the-other, where the first fill sends a second order and nothing is canceled.
questions.lesson_line: OCO keeps your two exits from both firing.
questions.simple: An OCO links two orders so that when one fills, the other is canceled right away.

questions.q: Tap the order link that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: My target and my stop cover the same 300 shares, linked as an ___ so one fill kills the other.
questions.why: OCO, one-cancels-the-other. Your target and your stop both cover the same 300 shares. Linked as an OCO, the stop is canceled as soon as the target fills. Without the link, a stop left behind could later sell shares you no longer own and open a short by accident.
questions.lesson_line: Two exits on one position: link them as an OCO.
questions.simple: OCO is the link, because it cancels the stop once the target fills, so both exits never fire.

questions.q: How should the two entries be set up?
questions.story: A stock trades at $21. A trader will buy a pullback to $20 or a breakout over $22.50, whichever comes first. They want only one position.
choices: OCO of buy limit $20, stop $22.50
Buy limit $20, buy stop $22.50
A bracket on the $20 buy limit
One stop-limit, $20 to $22.50
questions.why: An OCO with a buy limit at $20 and a buy stop at $22.50. Whichever fills first cancels the other, so both can't fill. The buy limit fills at $20 or lower. The buy stop sits above the price and triggers on a rise to $22.50.
questions.lesson_line: An OCO links two orders so only one of them can fill.

wrong.Buy limit $20, buy stop $22.50: Separate orders can both fill. A pop to $22.50, then a drop to $20, doubles the position.
wrong.A bracket on the $20 buy limit: A bracket attaches exits to one entry. It doesn't cancel the breakout entry.
wrong.One stop-limit, $20 to $22.50: Buy stops must sit above the price, and $20 is below it. One order can't be both entries.

questions.simple: An OCO, because it links the two entries so when one fills the other cancels, leaving one position.

deeper.trap: Two separate entry orders are not linked. If the stock pops to $22.50 and then drops back to $20, both fill and the position is twice the plan. An OCO pairs them so one executing cancels the other. Investopedia notes OCO orders are common in retracement and breakout trading.
deeper.counter: UCT enters differently. Our rule is that entries are market orders, and the stop still sits with the broker.

reasons: fixed before (f123 claim)
teaches resting limit and stop entries beside the owner's rule E57 (entries are market orders): flagged

questions.q: On an order ticket, what does the time in force set?
choices: How long the order stays live
The price that triggers it
How many shares can fill
When the trade settles
questions.answer: How long the order stays live
questions.why: How long the order stays live. Time in force is the time frame an order must happen within, and you pick it on the ticket. A day order cancels at the close if it hasn't filled. A good 'til canceled order stays active until it fills or you cancel it, within your broker's time limit.
questions.lesson_line: Every order has a clock. Check it before you send.

wrong.The price that triggers it: That's the stop price, its own field on a stop order. Time in force is about how long the order lives.
wrong.How many shares can fill: That's the quantity, plus size conditions like all-or-none.
wrong.When the trade settles: Time in force is the time frame the order itself must happen within. It sets nothing about settlement.

questions.simple: Time in force sets how long your order stays live, like today only or until you cancel it.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass; rebalanced again here

questions.q: If you don't set a time limit, your order is a day order.
questions.why: True. Unless you pick a time frame, an order is a Day order. It is good only during the trading day you enter it. If it doesn't fill, it generally cancels at the end of regular trading hours.
questions.lesson_line: No time limit chosen means today only.
questions.simple: True, because unless you choose a time frame, an order is a day order and lasts only that trading day.

questions.q: What happens to your order?
questions.story: At 2 p.m. you place a day order to buy at a $30.00 limit. It doesn't fill by the close. After hours, the stock trades at $29.80.
choices: Nothing, it expired at the close
It fills after hours near $29.80
It waits to fill at tomorrow's open
It becomes a market buy at the close
questions.answer: Nothing, it expired at the close
questions.why: Nothing, it expired at the close. A day order is good only during the trading day it is entered. If it doesn't fill, it generally cancels at the end of regular trading hours. It does not carry into the extended-hours session or the next day. So the $29.80 trade after hours can't fill it. If you still want the shares, enter a new order.
questions.lesson_line: A day order dies at the close. If you still want it, enter it again.

wrong.It fills after hours near $29.80: A day order doesn't carry into the extended-hours session. It was gone at the close.
wrong.It becomes a market buy at the close: A day limit order never turns into a market order. Unfilled at the end of regular hours, it generally cancels.
wrong.It waits to fill at tomorrow's open: That's what a GTC order would do. A day order doesn't carry to the next day.

questions.simple: Nothing happens, because an unfilled day order cancels at the close and does not carry into after-hours trading.

deeper.trap: The trap is seeing a price below your $30.00 limit after hours and assuming you bought. The SEC says day orders that don't execute generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours. They don't carry over to the extended hours session. Check your open orders after the close. A day order that missed is gone, not waiting.

questions.q: What does good 'til canceled (GTC) mean on an order?
choices: Live until filled or you cancel
Live only for today's session
Fill right away or cancel at once
Live for the rest of this week
questions.answer: Live until filled or you cancel
questions.why: Live until it fills or you cancel. The SEC says a GTC order lasts until it is executed in full or canceled. Unlike a day order, it carries past today's close.
questions.lesson_line: GTC outlives the day. Keep track of what you've left working.

wrong.Live for the rest of this week: GTC isn't a set week. It runs until it fills or you cancel.

questions.simple: GTC means the order stays live past today, until it fills or you cancel it.

questions.q: A GTC order can expire even if you never cancel it.
questions.why: True. The SEC says how long a GTC order can stay open may vary by brokerage firm. Fidelity expires open GTC orders 180 calendar days after they are placed. Schwab says brokers typically allow no more than 90 days.
questions.lesson_line: Good 'til canceled isn't forever. Know your broker's limit.
questions.simple: True, many brokers put a time limit on GTC orders, and it varies by broker, so check yours.

deeper.trap: An order you set months ago may be gone, or may still be live. Fidelity cancels open GTC orders after 180 calendar days. Investopedia says most brokers expire them after 30 to 90 days, to avoid a long-forgotten order suddenly being filled. Review what you have working.

reasons: broker time limits (180 days, 90 days) can change; no number is keyed
re-asked as True in wave8 to drop the absolute-word tell

questions.q: You send an immediate-or-cancel (IOC) order to buy 800 shares. Only 300 can fill right away. How many shares get canceled?
questions.why: 500. An immediate-or-cancel order fills whatever it can at once and cancels any unfilled balance. 800 less 300 filled leaves 500 canceled. Unlike fill-or-kill, IOC keeps the partial fill, so you own the 300 shares.
questions.lesson_line: IOC takes what's there now and walks away from the rest.
questions.simple: 500 shares cancel, because IOC keeps the 300 it can fill now and drops the rest of the 800.

deeper.counter: A fill-or-kill order on the same ticket would cancel all 800 shares. The SEC says FOK allows no partial execution: the whole order fills at once or none of it does. IOC keeps the 300 it could get.

reasons: computed key (calc)

choices: 500 shares
800 shares
1,100 shares
240,000 shares

wrong.800 shares: Canceled the whole order, which is fill-or-kill, not IOC.
wrong.1,100 shares: Added the filled shares to the order.
wrong.240,000 shares: Multiplied the two numbers instead of subtracting.

questions.q: Which instruction fits?
questions.story: You want 5,000 shares. You'll take them only if all 5,000 fill right now. Otherwise, forget it.
choices: Fill-or-kill (FOK)
Immediate-or-cancel (IOC)
All-or-none (AON)
Good 'til canceled (GTC)
questions.why: Fill-or-kill. An FOK order must be executed right away and in its entirety, or the whole order is canceled. No partial fill is allowed. IOC would keep any part that fills now. AON also refuses a partial, but it can stay active and wait.
questions.lesson_line: FOK: all of it, right now, or nothing.

wrong.Immediate-or-cancel (IOC): IOC keeps whatever part fills right away. You could end up with a partial.
wrong.All-or-none (AON): AON wants all of it too, but it can sit and wait. You said now or never.
wrong.Good 'til canceled (GTC): GTC is about how long the order lives. It says nothing about filling all at once.

questions.simple: Fill-or-kill fits, because it buys all 5,000 shares right now or cancels the whole order.

questions.q: What happens to each?
questions.story: Two orders to buy 1,000 shares. Only 400 are offered at your price right now. Order A is fill-or-kill. Order B is all-or-none.
choices: A cancels at once; B waits for all 1,000
Both buy 400 and cancel the rest
A buys 400 now; B cancels at once
Both wait until all 1,000 can fill
questions.answer: A cancels at once; B waits for all 1,000
questions.why: A cancels, B waits. Fill-or-kill must fill in full right away. With only 400 of the 1,000 shares offered, it is canceled at once and takes no partial. All-or-none also needs the full 1,000. Unlike FOK, it stays active until it fills or you cancel it.
questions.lesson_line: FOK and AON both refuse a partial. Only FOK refuses to wait.

wrong.Both buy 400 and cancel the rest: That's immediate-or-cancel. Neither order here accepts a partial fill.
wrong.A buys 400 now; B cancels at once: Backwards. Fill-or-kill never takes a partial, and all-or-none can wait.
wrong.Both wait until all 1,000 can fill: Fill-or-kill can't wait. It cancels at once if it can't fill in full.

questions.simple: Order A cancels at once because fill-or-kill can't wait, while order B waits since all-or-none can stay open.

deeper.trap: Both orders refuse a partial fill, so it is easy to treat them as the same. The difference is time. The SEC says an FOK must execute immediately in its entirety. An AON that can't fill right away remains active until it is executed or canceled. All or nothing, but able to wait: AON. All or nothing, right now: FOK.

questions.q: Tap the order that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: I want my buy filled at the end of today's regular session, so I'll send a ___ order.
questions.why: Market-on-close. It is an order to be executed at the closing price. Any part not executed in the closing trade is canceled. Market-on-open is the same idea at the start of regular trading hours.
questions.lesson_line: On-close orders trade the closing price, or not at all.
questions.simple: Market-on-close is the order meant to fill at the day's closing price, and any unfilled part cancels.

questions.q: On your order screen, what does a fill mean?
choices: An executed order, or its price
An order waiting to trade
Shares left after a cancel
The total shares traded today
questions.answer: An executed order, or its price
questions.why: An executed order, or the price it executed at. Nasdaq's glossary gives both meanings. Filled means the order traded. An order still waiting to trade is not a fill.
questions.lesson_line: A fill is a done trade. Until then, it's just an order.

wrong.An order waiting to trade: That's a working order. Nothing has traded yet.
wrong.Shares left after a cancel: Those didn't fill. A fill is what did trade.
wrong.The total shares traded today: That's the day's volume, for everyone. A fill is your own order.

questions.simple: A fill is an order that traded, or the price it traded at.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (Nasdaq f68, Tier 1)
fixed before (circular wrong note reworded)

questions.q: One order can fill at more than one price.
questions.why: True. Parts of a large order can execute at different prices when one price doesn't hold enough shares. Limit orders can also fill in parts until complete. Check your average fill price, not just the first fill.
questions.lesson_line: Big order, thin price: expect several fills and check the average.
questions.simple: True, because a big order can run out of shares at one price and fill the rest at other prices.

questions.q: What is a partial fill?
choices: Only part of your order executed
Your order filled at a worse price
Your broker refused the order
Your order filled after the close
questions.answer: Only part of your order executed
questions.why: Only part of your order executed. Some shares filled and the rest did not. What happens to the rest depends on the order. An IOC cancels it at once. An unfilled day order cancels at the close. A GTC order keeps working. All-or-none and fill-or-kill exist to avoid a partial fill.
questions.lesson_line: Check the filled shares, not just the order. A partial can leave you half in.

wrong.Your order filled at a worse price: That's slippage. An order can fill in full and still fill worse.
wrong.Your broker refused the order: That's a rejected order. Nothing filled.
wrong.Your order filled after the close: That's an after-hours fill. It says nothing about how much filled.

questions.simple: A partial fill means only some of your shares traded, and the rest were canceled or are still waiting.

questions.q: Which word names what happened?
questions.story: A trader says after the open: "Only got 300 of my 1,000 before it ran from my limit." Nothing else filled.
choices: Partial fill
Slippage
Rejected order
Fill-or-kill
questions.why: Partial fill. Only 300 of the 1,000 shares executed, at the limit or better, before price ran away. A limit order fills only at its price or better. Once price moved past it, the rest didn't fill. The price was fine. The size fell short.
questions.lesson_line: A limit protects your price, so on a runner you may get only part.

wrong.Slippage: Slippage is a worse price than expected. Here the price was fine. The size fell short.
wrong.Rejected order: A rejected order fills nothing. This one got 300 shares.
wrong.Fill-or-kill: A fill-or-kill order would have canceled. It never takes part of an order.

questions.simple: It is a partial fill, because only 300 of the 1,000 shares traded before the price ran from the limit.

deeper.trap: Don't call this slippage. Slippage is about price, a fill better or worse than you expected. Here the price was fine and the size fell short. The cure differs too. Limit orders reduce bad slippage, while a partial fill is the price a limit order pays for its control. Then check whether the rest of the order is still working.

questions.q: Where do you stand?
questions.story: Your GTC limit order to buy 2,000 shares has 600 filled. The stock then moved up and away from your limit.
choices: You own 600; 1,400 are still working
The order is done; 1,400 were canceled
You own 2,000 at an average price
Nothing counts until all 2,000 fill
questions.why: You own 600, and 1,400 are still working. A GTC order lasts until it is executed in full or canceled. A plain limit order can fill in parts, so the 600 are yours and the rest waits at your limit. It fills only if price comes back to it. It stays open until you cancel, within your broker's time limit.
questions.lesson_line: After a partial, decide: leave the rest working or cancel it. Don't forget it's there.

wrong.The order is done; 1,400 were canceled: That's how a day order ends at the close, or an IOC right away. A GTC keeps working.
wrong.You own 2,000 at an average price: Only 600 traded. You don't own shares that never filled.
wrong.Nothing counts until all 2,000 fill: That's all-or-none. A plain limit order can fill in parts.

questions.simple: You own 600 shares, and the other 1,400 stay open at your limit because a GTC order lasts until filled or canceled.

deeper.trap: The forgotten remainder. A GTC order keeps working after a partial. Weeks later the other 1,400 shares can fill when price comes back, maybe after your reason to buy is gone. The SEC notes that how long a GTC order can stay open varies by broker. After a partial, decide on purpose: keep the rest working or cancel it.

questions.q: What is slippage on a trade?
choices: Your fill vs. the price you expected
The gap between bid and ask
The day's high minus the day's low
A price gap between trading days
questions.answer: Your fill vs. the price you expected
questions.why: Your fill versus the price you expected. Investopedia defines slippage as the difference between a trade's expected price and its executed price. Nasdaq frames it as expected versus actual cost.
questions.lesson_line: Slippage measures your fill against the price you expected.

wrong.The gap between bid and ask: That's the spread. Slippage is the gap between your expected price and your fill.
wrong.The day's high minus the day's low: That's the day's range. It isn't about your order at all.
wrong.A price gap between trading days: That's a gap on the chart. A gap can cause slippage on a stop, but it isn't slippage.

questions.simple: Slippage is the gap between the price you expected and the price you actually got.

reasons: fixed before (f69 claim)
two published definitions (conflicts note); the key uses the price sense both cover

questions.q: You send a market buy for 1,000 shares with the ask at $15.20. They fill at an average of $15.29. What did slippage cost you?
questions.why: $90. A market buy generally fills at or near the ask, so $15.20 was the price you expected. You paid an average of $15.29, which is $0.09 a share more. Times 1,000 shares is $90. A large order can fill in parts at several prices.
questions.lesson_line: A big market order can fill at several prices. Check your average fill, not just the quote.
questions.simple: It cost $90, because you paid $15.29 a share instead of the $15.20 ask, on 1,000 shares.

reasons: computed key (calc)
fixed before (why reworded for an average fill)

wrong.$0.09: Gave the slippage per share and skipped the 1,000 shares.
wrong.$15,290: Gave the total price paid, not the extra cost.

questions.q: Slippage can work in your favor.
questions.why: True. Slippage is the difference between the price you expected and the price you got. It can be positive, negative or zero. Positive slippage means a better price than expected. The SEC calls a fill better than the quote price improvement, an opportunity but not a guarantee.
questions.lesson_line: Hope for better fills. Plan for worse ones.
questions.simple: True, because slippage is any gap from the price you expected, and sometimes the fill comes in better.

deeper.counter: Positive slippage is real, but you can't plan on it. Investopedia notes slippage is most common in volatile or thin markets. A limit order caps the bad side, since it fills only at your price or better. Plan your risk on the worse fill, and treat a better one as a bonus.

questions.q: Where is slippage on a stop most likely?
questions.story: A trader holds four stocks, the same size in each. Each has a sell stop the same distance below its price.
choices: A thinly traded stock on big news
A heavily traded stock on big news
A thinly traded stock on a quiet day
A heavily traded stock on a quiet day
questions.answer: A thinly traded stock on big news
questions.why: A thinly traded stock on big news. Investopedia says slippage is most common in volatile or low-liquidity markets. The SEC says a triggered stop fills at the prices of available liquidity. This one is both fast and thin.
questions.lesson_line: Slippage is most common when price moves fast and few orders are there.

wrong.A heavily traded stock on big news: Fast, but deep. It has one driver of slippage, speed, but not thin liquidity.
wrong.A thinly traded stock on a quiet day: Thin, but calm. It has one driver of slippage, thin liquidity, but not speed.
wrong.A heavily traded stock on a quiet day: Deep and calm. Neither driver of slippage is there.

questions.simple: The thin stock on big news, because slippage is most common when price moves fast and few orders are there.

deeper.trap: The same stop distance does not mean the same risk. A stop is a trigger for a market order, and that order takes whatever liquidity is there. FINRA warns a stop in a fast market may fill significantly different from its stop price. In a thin stock on big news, the fill can land well past the stop.
deeper.counter: We avoid the thin name in the first place. Our rule trades only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

reasons: judgment key: no source ranks speed against thinness, so the key is the only choice with both (conflicts note)

questions.q: In a short sale, what are you doing?
choices: Selling borrowed shares, rebuy later
Selling shares on the day you buy them
Selling at a loss to cut risk
Selling part of a winning position
questions.why: Selling borrowed shares and buying them back later. The SEC defines a short sale as selling stock you don't own, delivered with borrowed shares. You close it by buying the shares back and returning them. You lose if the price rises.
questions.lesson_line: Short means you sold first. You still owe the shares back.

wrong.Selling shares on the day you buy them: That's a day trade. You owned the shares first.
wrong.Selling at a loss to cut risk: That's taking a loss on shares you own.
wrong.Selling part of a winning position: That's selling partials, trimming shares you own.

questions.simple: A short sale means you sell borrowed shares now and buy them back later, hoping the price falls.

reasons: fixed before (f103 added)

questions.q: What is it called when a broker checks that shares can be borrowed for a short?
choices: Locate
Margin call
Short interest
Buy to cover
questions.why: Locate. Regulation SHO requires the broker to have reasonable grounds that the shares can be borrowed. That way they can be delivered when due. The SEC calls this check a locate.
questions.lesson_line: No locate, no short. That's the rule, not a broker courtesy.

wrong.Margin call: A margin call asks you to add cash or securities when your account falls short.
wrong.Short interest: Short interest is the total of open short positions in a stock.
wrong.Buy to cover: That's the order that closes a short.

questions.simple: It is called a locate, the broker's check that the shares can be borrowed for the short.

reasons: a regulation that can change (Rule 203 of Regulation SHO; current eCFR text cited)

questions.q: Your broker can get the locate after your short sale goes through, as long as it's the same day.
questions.why: False. Under Regulation SHO, a broker must have reasonable grounds to believe the shares can be borrowed and delivered when due. It needs that before it effects the short sale. This locate must be made and documented before the short, not after, whatever the day.
questions.lesson_line: The locate comes first. Then the short.
questions.simple: False, because the broker must have good reason to believe the shares can be borrowed before your short goes through.

reasons: a regulatory rule (Regulation SHO Rule 203) that can change; current eCFR text cited

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A short seller sells shares they don't own, so they first ___ them, usually from their broker.
questions.why: Borrow. A short sale is delivered with borrowed shares, and your broker usually lends them to you. The loan can carry a fee. Schwab says the most liquid shares may cost nothing and the least liquid more than 100% a year.
questions.lesson_line: A short starts with a loan of shares. Check what the borrow costs.
questions.simple: Borrow, because you sell shares you do not own, so you borrow them first, usually from your broker.

questions.q: Your platform flags a stock as hard to borrow. What does that tell you?
choices: Few shares free to lend for shorts
Shorting it is banned by law
It can't trade until the open
It's too costly to buy outright
questions.answer: Few shares free to lend for shorts
questions.why: Few shares are free to lend. A hard-to-borrow list names stocks that are hard to obtain for short sales. They may carry higher loan fees, and a short order may be refused. Brokers update these lists daily.
questions.lesson_line: Hard to borrow can mean a higher fee to short, or a short order refused.

wrong.Shorting it is banned by law: It's about the broker's supply of shares to lend, not a law. A short may still go through, at a higher fee.
wrong.It can't trade until the open: Borrow has nothing to do with trading hours.
wrong.It's too costly to buy outright: Buying doesn't need a borrow. The flag is about shorting.

questions.simple: It means few shares are free to lend for shorting, so the fee can be high or the short refused.

reasons: fixed before ('can be high' restored)

questions.q: Which word most likely explains it?
questions.story: You try to short a small, heavily shorted stock. Your broker rejects the order. Yesterday the same order went through.
choices: Hard to borrow
Partial fill
Negative slippage
Time in force
questions.why: Hard to borrow. In a small, heavily shorted stock the shares to lend can run out. A short order in a hard-to-borrow stock may be refused. Brokers update those lists daily, so yesterday's order can pass and today's fail.
questions.lesson_line: On a crowded short, the borrow can vanish from one day to the next. Check it before you plan the trade.

wrong.Partial fill: Nothing filled. The order was refused.
wrong.Negative slippage: Slippage needs a fill. Yours never traded.
wrong.Time in force: Time in force sets how long an order lasts. Nothing in the story points to it.

questions.simple: Hard to borrow, because when shares to lend run out a broker can refuse a short, and that can change overnight.

deeper.trap: A stock you shorted easily last week can be closed to new shorts today. Brokers update hard-to-borrow lists daily. Schwab notes shares can be hard to locate when demand is high or few shares exist. A broker can also refuse a short for other reasons, such as no margin agreement. Read the rejection message.

reasons: hard-to-borrow status changes daily; hedged 'most likely' key because other refusal causes exist (conflicts note)

questions.q: Your borrow fee is set when you go short, and it holds until you cover.
questions.why: False. Schwab says the cost to borrow a stock can change frequently with supply and demand. Fidelity says short fees may change, sometimes significantly and without warning. A fee that was low at entry can rise while you hold.
questions.lesson_line: Check the borrow rate while you hold a short, not just when you enter.
questions.simple: False, the fee to borrow can change while you are short, sometimes a lot and with no warning.

questions.q: You're short 200 shares. Which order action closes the position?
choices: Buy to cover
Sell to close
Sell short
Buy to open
questions.why: Buy to cover. You close a short by buying the shares back and returning them to the lender. On the ticket, sell short opens the position and a buy to cover order closes it. Sell to close needs shares you own, and you own none. Selling short again makes the short bigger.
questions.lesson_line: Sell short to open. Buy to cover to close.

wrong.Sell short: That sells more borrowed shares and makes the short bigger.
wrong.Sell to close: Selling never closes a short. You own no shares here. You owe 200, and a short closes by buying them back.
wrong.Buy to open: You want to close the short, not open anything. A short is closed by buying the shares back with a buy to cover order.

questions.simple: Buy to cover closes it, because a short is ended by buying the 200 shares back.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: It ran against my short, so I bought the shares back to ___ at a loss.
questions.why: Cover. Buying shares back to close a short is short covering. You bought back above the price you shorted at, so covering locked in a loss.
questions.lesson_line: Covering is the buy that ends a short.
questions.simple: Cover is the word, because buying shares back to close a short is called covering.

questions.q: You short 200 shares at $18.00. A squeeze hits and you buy to cover at $27.40. How much did you lose, before costs?
questions.why: $1,880. On a short you lose what the price rose. $27.40 less $18.00 is $9.40 a share. Times 200 shares is $1,880. Covering above the price you shorted at is a loss. Costs such as interest on the borrowed shares would add to it.
questions.lesson_line: A short loses as price rises, and price can keep rising. Have your buy stop in.
questions.simple: You lost $1,880, because the price rose from $18.00 to $27.40 on the 200 shares you were short.

reasons: computed key (calc)

wrong.$9.40: Gave the loss per share and skipped the 200 shares.

questions.q: What is a short squeeze?
choices: Short covering lifts the price fast
Shorts piling in sink the price
A stock stuck in a tight range
A broker forcing longs to sell
questions.answer: Short covering lifts the price fast
questions.why: Short covering lifts the price fast. The SEC defines a short squeeze as pressure on short sellers to cover. A sharp price rise or a hard borrow causes it. Their buying adds upward pressure, which can squeeze them harder. It is a rise driven by shorts buying back, not a drop.
questions.lesson_line: In a squeeze, the shorts become the buyers.

wrong.A stock stuck in a tight range: That's a tight range. Nobody is being forced to buy.
wrong.A broker forcing longs to sell: That describes forced selling by owners. A squeeze is pressure on short sellers to buy back.
wrong.Shorts piling in sink the price: That's the reverse. In a squeeze the short sellers are under pressure, and their buying back lifts the price.

questions.simple: A short squeeze is when shorts rush to buy back shares, and their buying pushes the price up even faster.

reasons: choices rewritten in the 2026-11-10 variety pass

questions.q: Heavy short interest means a short squeeze is coming.
questions.why: False. Heavy short interest means many people believe the price will fall. It does not mean it will rise. A squeeze needs pressure that forces shorts to cover, such as a sharp rise or a hard borrow. The SEC warns that claims of an imminent squeeze may be false.
questions.lesson_line: Short interest is a crowd, not a catalyst. I'd want a real reason to own it.
questions.simple: False, because heavy short interest only shows many people expect a fall, and it does not force anyone to buy.

deeper.trap: Squeeze stories sell. The SEC warns of claims that an imminent short squeeze will force shorts to cover. It says these claims in fact may be false. Investopedia adds that anyone buying for a squeeze should have other, better reasons to think the price will rise. A crowded short is a crowd's opinion, not a catalyst.

questions.q: What's the move?
questions.story: You're short a heavily shorted stock. It gaps up on news and keeps climbing as shorts buy back. It's just under your buy stop now.
choices: Let the stop take you out
Cancel the stop and wait it out
Raise the stop a bit to give it room
Wait for the close to decide
questions.answer: Let the stop take you out
questions.why: Let the stop take you out. The stop is there for this. In a squeeze, shorts buying back push the price higher, which can cause an even greater squeeze. A short's loss has no ceiling, since a stock can keep rising. Canceling or raising the stop takes on more risk just as it grows. In a fast move, the fill can come in above your stop.
questions.lesson_line: On a short, honor the buy stop. A squeeze can keep running, and the loss has no ceiling.

wrong.Cancel the stop and wait it out: That removes your only exit while the loss has no limit.
wrong.Wait for the close to decide: A stop doesn't wait for the close, and neither does a squeeze.
wrong.Raise the stop a bit to give it room: That widens the loss you set before the trade. Schwab's advice is to decide how much you would lose ahead of time.

questions.simple: Let the stop close the short, because a squeeze can keep pushing the price up and a short's loss has no limit.

deeper.trap: The urge in a squeeze is to hold for a pullback, or to short more at a better price. Both raise risk while shorts are being forced to buy. The SEC notes that their rush to cover can cause an even greater squeeze. Schwab's advice is to decide how much you would be comfortable losing before the trade. Then let the order you placed do its job.

reasons: judgment key that agrees with the owner's rulebook A4 and D41 (the stop is the exit, a real stop order with the broker)

questions.q: What does short interest measure?
choices: Total open short positions in a stock
Shares sold short in a single day
The yearly fee to borrow a stock
Shares the company bought back
questions.answer: Total open short positions in a stock
questions.why: Total open short positions in a stock. The SEC calls short interest the aggregate number of open short positions. FINRA says it is a snapshot on a given settlement date, and that short sale volume is not the same thing.
questions.lesson_line: Short interest counts positions still open. Daily short volume is a different number.

wrong.Shares sold short in a single day: That's short sale volume. FINRA says it is not the same as short interest.
wrong.The yearly fee to borrow a stock: That's the borrow fee, the interest on the stock loan.
wrong.Shares the company bought back: That's a buyback. It has nothing to do with shorts.

questions.simple: Short interest is the total number of short positions still open in a stock, counted on a set date.

reasons: fixed before ('per day' fee note corrected)

questions.q: Next week XYZ trades down to $47.50. What happens?
questions.story: Your order screen shows: Sell 200 XYZ, type Stop, stop price $47.50, time in force GTC. XYZ closes today at $49.
choices: It turns into a market sell order
Nothing, it expired at today's close
It sells exactly at $47.50 a share
It becomes a limit order at $47.50
questions.answer: It turns into a market sell order
questions.why: It turns into a market order to sell. The time in force is GTC, so the order stays live past today until it fills or you cancel it. When XYZ reaches the $47.50 stop price, the stop becomes a market order. The fill can come in below $47.50. The stop price is a trigger, not a promised price.
questions.lesson_line: Read the order type and the time in force together. They decide what happens, and when.

wrong.Nothing, it expired at today's close: That's what a day order would do. This one is GTC.
wrong.It sells exactly at $47.50 a share: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised price.
wrong.It becomes a limit order at $47.50: That's a stop-limit. The type here is a plain stop.

questions.simple: It becomes a market sell, because GTC keeps the stop alive past today and the stop fires at $47.50.

deeper.trap: Two fields decide this order: the type and the time in force. Read only the type and you might think it died at today's close. Read only the price and you might expect exactly $47.50. GTC keeps it live past today, and a plain stop goes to market at its trigger. If XYZ gaps below $47.50, the fill can land well under the stop.

questions.q: What is this order for?
questions.story: Your order screen shows: Buy to cover 100 ABC, type Stop, stop price $31.00. ABC trades at $28.50.
choices: Protecting a short from a rise
Buying a fresh breakout above $31
Covering the short right now
Shorting more ABC if it hits $31
questions.answer: Protecting a short from a rise
questions.why: Protecting a short from a rise. Buy to cover is the order that closes a short. A buy stop sits above the current price and sends a market buy only if the stock rises to it. At $28.50, nothing happens unless ABC reaches $31.00.
questions.lesson_line: Buy to cover with a stop above the price: that's a short's protective stop.

wrong.Covering the short right now: It's a stop. It waits, and only buys if ABC rises to $31.
wrong.Shorting more ABC if it hits $31: Adding to a short takes a sell short order. Buy to cover only closes a short.
wrong.Buying a fresh breakout above $31: A breakout entry would be a plain buy. Buy to cover only closes a short.

questions.simple: It guards a short, because a buy to cover stop above the price only buys back if the stock climbs to $31.00.

deeper.trap: 'Buy' on the screen does not always mean a new long. Buy to cover only closes shares you are short. Read the action and the type together: Buy to cover plus Stop, above the price, is a short's protective stop. FINRA says stop-buy orders on a short limit losses if the price rises.

questions.q: What does our rule say to do?
choices: Skip the short on this stock
Short it and count the fee in
Short it once the locate clears
Skip every short in its group
questions.answer: Skip the short on this stock
questions.why: Skip the short. Our rule is to skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow or the borrow fee is high. Hard to borrow can mean higher loan fees or a refused order.
questions.lesson_line: Hard to borrow or a high borrow fee: we skip the short.
questions.simple: Skip it, because our rule is to skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow.

wrong.Short it and count the fee in: Pricing in the fee isn't our rule. We skip a short when the borrow fee is high, too.
wrong.Short it once the locate clears: A locate only says the shares can be borrowed. Our rule still skips a hard-to-borrow short.
wrong.Skip every short in its group: Our rule is about this stock. It says nothing about other stocks in its group.

questions.q: By default, what makes us sell a winner we're trailing?
choices: A close below the 9 or 20 EMA
Its first touch of the 9 EMA
A trailing stop a set percent under it
A stop moved up under each day's low
questions.answer: A close below the 9 or 20 EMA
questions.why: A close below the 9 or 20 EMA. Our default trail is the 9 EMA for fast movers and the 20 EMA for steadier ones. We sell on a close below it, not on a touch. A trailing stop order is a broker tool this lesson teaches, but it is not our default trail.
questions.lesson_line: We trail with the 9 or 20 EMA and sell on a close below it.

wrong.A trailing stop a set percent under it: That's a trailing stop order, a broker tool. Our default trail is the 9 or 20 EMA.
wrong.A stop moved up under each day's low: Our default trail is an average, not each day's low. We sell on a close below the 9 or 20 EMA.
wrong.Its first touch of the 9 EMA: A touch is not enough. Our rule sells on a close below the average.

questions.simple: By default we sell a trailed winner when it closes below its 9 or 20 EMA.

conflicts: GTC time limits differ by broker and by source: the SEC bulletin says the limit 'may vary based on the brokerage firm'; Fidelity's FAQ says open GTC orders expire after 180 calendar days; Schwab says brokers typically allow no more than 90 days; Investopedia says most brokers use 30 to 90 days. No question keys a number. q30's why and w2 say 'within your broker's time limit', and q31 keys only that the limit varies.

Default order type: FINRA's Order Types page and the SEC's Market Order glossary both say brokers typically enter a market order unless you specify otherwise. Individual platforms' ticket presets were not surveyed, so q02 is keyed on the official wording ('typically') and its why tells the member to check their own ticket.

Slippage has two published definitions. Nasdaq's glossary (Tier 1): the difference between estimated and actual transaction costs, 'usually' from price difference or spread and commission revisions. Investopedia (Tier 2): expected price vs executed price. Every slippage key uses the price sense, which Nasdaq's 'price difference' covers; the commission is never offered as a wrong answer for what slippage is, so neither definition is contradicted.

Bracket naming: Schwab and Interactive Brokers call entry-plus-linked-exits a 'bracket'; Fidelity calls the same structure one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other (OTOCO). Questions use 'bracket' and cite Fidelity's OTOCO text as the same structure (q23).

Trailing stop wording: the SEC bulletin defines a trailing stop as 'a stop or stop limit order'; Schwab's advanced-orders article says trailing stops 'are not orders per se' but a way to move stops. The file follows the SEC definition; q17's distractor 'A stop that turns into a limit order' is explained as the stop-limit definition, since what makes a stop trailing is the moving price (a trailing stop-limit exists, per the SEC and thinkorswim pages).

Outdated lines seen and NOT used: Fidelity's FAQ short-sale example says 'Three trading days later, on settlement date' and Nasdaq's 'Execution' glossary says stocks settle in three days (US settlement has been T+1 since May 2024); the SEC Key Points page says the locate is 'usually done two days before settlement' (written for T+2); Investopedia's squeeze page speaks of short positions' 'expiration date' (a stock short has none). No fact or question relies on them.

Stop triggers: the SEC says some firms trigger stops on last-sale prices and others on quotes. q13's story has the stock trade at $44.80 for a few minutes, through a $45 sell stop, so the key holds under either standard; no question asks which standard a broker uses.

Locate sources: the SEC's 'Key Points About Regulation SHO' page (last modified 2022) explains the locate in plain words; the current rule text (eCFR, 17 CFR 242.203(b)(1)) is cited beside it so the rule is checked as it stands today. Both say the same thing: the borrow condition comes before the short sale.

Rejected short (q50): a broker can also refuse a short order for reasons the unit does not teach (for example the Rule 201 short-sale price test, or an account without margin). None of those is a choice, and among the four words offered only hard to borrow can block a short, so the question asks which word 'most likely' explains it.

Slippage judgment (q44): the sources name two drivers, fast markets (FINRA, SEC, Investopedia) and thin liquidity (Investopedia, SEC 'prices of available liquidity'). No source ranks them, so the key is the only choice with both; each wrong choice carries one driver or neither, and its note says which.
